name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,234

clue.text: Denies bodice ripped in act of insubordination

indicators.note: something ripped is torn apart, so the letters before it are pulled to pieces and rebuilt

blocks.note: the twelve letters of both words taken together

explanation.surface: A defiant wearer refuses the bodice and tears it apart in protest.
explanation.walkthrough: The ripped bodice suggests a romance novel, but 'ripped' just tears up the letters of the first two words, which make exactly twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing to obey orders from those in authority is exactly what insubordination involves, so the two terms are synonyms.

clue.text: Shop’s nice deals set in motion

indicators.note: letters that are moving about do not stay put, so they end up in a new order

blocks.note: the twelve letters of the three words together

explanation.surface: A store has started a run of attractive bargains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop's' reads as a possessive, but the 's is just 'is' linking the definition to the wordplay; 'set' belongs to the letters being shuffled, not to the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is a type of retail store selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared foods.

clue.text: Certain about trait regularly noticed in level of achievement

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
to be about something is to go around it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: certain means sure
the first, third and fifth letters of trait

explanation.surface: Someone is confident a particular quality shows in what a person has achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' means every other letter, starting from the first; the container is split after its first letter to take the three.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature means the standing or reputation someone has earned through accomplishments, the figurative sense of height.

clue.text: Newlywed losing grand in card game

indicators.note: whatever is lost is no longer there, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: bridge is a card game played in pairs
G is short for grand, a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: A newly married person loses a thousand dollars at the card table.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the G out of BRIDGE and BRIDE is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride is a woman on her wedding day or just married, so she is a newlywed.

clue.text: Figure — like it a lot

blocks.note: first meaning: a numeral from 0 to 9
second meaning: read as two words, slang for enjoying something greatly

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer into two words, DIG IT, the slang phrase for really liking something; crosswords often ignore spacing like this.
explanation.definitionFit: A digit is a single numerical figure, and 'dig it' is informal for strongly approving of something.

clue.text: Sixteen becoming involved, extremely valuable, far-reaching

indicators.note: things that get involved become tangled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: the number written out as a word
the first and last letters of valuable

explanation.surface: A sixteen-year-old gets caught up in something extremely valuable with wide consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of the number itself are rearranged; the ends of 'valuable' are then tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extensive covers a large area or range, so it reaches far and wide in its effects.

clue.text: Nice ref, not coy, put out sweets?

indicators.note: being put out means being upset or disturbed, so the letters are knocked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the thirteen letters of the four words together

explanation.surface: A friendly referee, not at all shy, hands out treats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like 'handed out', but it is the anagram signal; the question mark flags the playful picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Confectionery is the collective name for candies, chocolates and other sugary treats.

clue.text: Annoy noble, taking in septic tank at first

indicators.note: to take something in is to receive it inside, so one piece goes within another
what comes at first is the opening letter, so only the starts of the words are kept

blocks.note: a peer is a member of the nobility
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is bothered by having to deal with a septic tank.
explanation.walkthrough: PEER is split in the middle to take in the two initials: PE-ST-ER.
explanation.definitionFit: To pester someone is to bother them persistently, the same as irritating or annoying them.

clue.text: Up, making case in court, not quiet at first?

indicators.note: saying 'not' excludes something, so a letter is removed from the word
at first points to the very beginning, so the letter removed is the opening one

blocks.note: pleading is arguing a case before a judge
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A lawyer gets up to argue a case, but there is nothing quiet about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' says where the quiet letter goes from: drop the opening P of PLEADING. 'Up' looks like a direction, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A team that is up by two goals is ahead in the contest, which means it is in front, winning the game.

clue.text: Some getting easement in shade

indicators.note: some of something is only a part of it, so the letters are a portion of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone obtains a right of way over land, with some shade thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: geTTING Easement holds the answer across the word break; an easement is a legal right to use someone else's land.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinge is a slight trace of colour, the same as a shade or hint of a hue.

clue.text: Slide into swimming pool in hotel, attractive on outside

indicators.note: a piece placed on the outside surrounds whatever else is given, so it wraps around

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
cute means attractive

explanation.surface: A hotel's pool has a waterslide that looks good from outside.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long opening phrase; CUTE goes around H after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A chute is a steep sloping channel down which swimmers whoosh into the water.

clue.text: Cheers northern chap’s touching line

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks
N is the abbreviation for northern
a gent is a man or chap

explanation.surface: A northern man's farewell is touching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' as thanks gives TA, the British informal word; the 's is 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a tangent is a straight line that meets a curve at a single point without crossing it.

clue.text: Twitter abandoning core elements? Finish to be widely discussed

indicators.note: dropping everything from the core leaves only the two outermost letters of the word

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Twitter
the end is the finish

explanation.surface: A social media site gives up its core features, and the end of it gets everyone talking.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase: to trend online is to be the subject everyone is posting about.
explanation.definitionFit: On social media a topic that trends is one being talked about by large numbers of users at once.

clue.text: Merit of French tennis shot

blocks.note: de is French for of
the serve is the shot that starts a tennis point

explanation.surface: Praising the quality of a French player's tennis stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merit' looks like a noun but is the verb: to merit something is to have earned it.
explanation.definitionFit: To deserve a reward is to have earned it, the same as being worthy of it.

clue.text: Hint: it’s a dog

blocks.note: first meaning: a tip or suggestion
second meaning: a gun dog breed that stands still aiming its nose at game

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a disappointed verdict on a clue being a dud; the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A helpful tip can be called a useful piece of guidance, and a gun dog breed is also named for showing hunters where game lies.

clue.text: Notice location for the most part north of a road

indicators.note: most but not all of something means the last letter is cut off
in a down entry what is north sits above, so it comes first

blocks.note: a place is a location
taken as written
Rd is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A sign showing a place a little north of a highway.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'north of' means the first piece sits above, so it is written first.
explanation.definitionFit: A placard is a large printed sign or poster put up in public, which is a kind of notice.

clue.text: Second joint phase rearranged in good order

indicators.note: rearranged means put in a different order, so these letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
the hip is a joint of the body
taken as written before being reshuffled

explanation.surface: A second stage of a hip-replacement recovery goes well after being reorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' wants to be a shared venture, but it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipshape describes something tidy and well arranged, as everything on a well-run ship must be.

clue.text: Inspire one making bold, unusual, effort at the outset

indicators.note: the outset is the very start, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
the first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Encouraging someone to make a bold, unconventional attempt from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas break up the phrase so it looks like a list of qualities; only the initials count.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue someone with courage is to fill them with that feeling, much as inspiring them would.

clue.text: Frequently one feels tense initially

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so the starting letters are kept

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A person often feels nervous at the start of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is not a number here; it is the first of three words whose initials are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Oft is a poetic or old-fashioned word meaning often, which is the same as frequently.

clue.text: Handle difficult IT lessons? Not entirely

indicators.note: something not taken entirely is only partly present, so the letters are a part of the phrase before

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the second into the third

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they can cope with hard computing classes, and admits only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a verb meaning cope with; it is a noun, slang for a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A handle is informal for a name someone goes by, and a title is a name or form of address.

clue.text: Financial predicament means Starmer must reform, bringing in billions?

indicators.note: to reform is to form anew, so the letters are rebuilt in another order
to bring something in is to put it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
the surname taken as letters
B is the abbreviation for billions

explanation.surface: A budget crisis forces the British prime minister, Keir Starmer, to change course and raise billions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means' looks like a link word, but it belongs to the letters being reshuffled; Keir Starmer is the UK prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial embarrassment is the established idiom for being short of money, a money predicament.

clue.text: Prescribe stage scenery

blocks.note: first meaning: to fix or lay down, as a task is assigned
second meaning: the constructed backdrop of a play

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a director's instruction about scenery; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher can fix homework for a class, and the built scenery of a theatre production has the same name.

clue.text: Support ultimately continued use of the loan word

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letters are kept

blocks.clueFragment: continued use of the loan word
blocks.note: the last letters of all six words

explanation.surface: Backing the ongoing use of a word borrowed from another language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' seems to apply to one word, but it covers all six words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To defend a position or person is to argue for them, the same as backing or supporting them.

clue.text: Herb, formerly your setter

blocks.note: thy is the old form of your
setters often refer to themselves as 'your setter'

explanation.surface: Herb used to be the setter, as if it were someone's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name, but it is the plant; the setter refers to themself, giving ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is an aromatic garden plant used in cooking, which makes it a culinary herb.
